# Sync new Shopify orders into Airtable

**Pattern:** Event -> map -> idempotent upsert · **Level:** Production · **Trigger:** Shopify webhook

## What it does
On every orders/create webhook, upserts a normalised row into an Airtable Orders table matched on Order ID, with an errors table for failures.

## Why it exists
Airtable is where a lot of ops and finance teams actually work. This gives them a live, no-code orders table they control — without polling and without duplicate rows on webhook retries.

## Main flow
On New Shopify Order -> Map Order to Columns -> Summarise Line Items -> Upsert Order in Airtable (failure -> Airtable errors table).

## Use it for
- A no-code Airtable orders dashboard
- Feeding an Airtable CRM/fulfilment view
- Live order data for staff without Shopify access

## You get
- Orders in Airtable within seconds
- Idempotent upsert — retries never duplicate
- Failures logged, never dropped

## Before first run
Connect credentials: Shopify Admin API access token; Airtable Personal Access Token.
Colour key: 🟦 entry · 🟫 app I/O · ⬜ logic · 🟩 output · 🟥 error rail.
Each node has its own doc card underneath — read those before editing.

## Try it now
This is event-driven; sample orders are pinned so the whole pipeline runs with no credential. Sample data is pinned on the trigger, so hit **Execute Workflow** to watch it flow end to end before attaching a single credential. Right-click → Unpin when you go live.

## Credentials setup

Credentials are never bundled in a template. Every node that talks to an external service needs its own connection before the first real run — open the node, click the Credential dropdown, choose **Create new**.

**Shopify Admin API access token**
Shopify Admin → Settings → Apps and sales channels → Develop apps → create an app → Admin API access token.
_Gotcha:_ Grant read_orders / read_products / read_customers as needed; the webhook trigger silently fails to register without the matching read scope.

**Airtable Personal Access Token**
Airtable → Builder hub → Personal access tokens → Create a token with data.records:read and data.records:write scopes on the base you're syncing. Paste it into n8n's Airtable Token credential.
_Gotcha:_ Field names are case-sensitive and must match your table's columns exactly, or writes fail with 422 UNKNOWN_FIELD_NAME.

Set each credential up once; it is reusable across every workflow in your instance.

## Troubleshooting

**Nothing happens when the event should fire**
Cause: The workflow is still a draft, or its trigger is inactive.
Fix: Publish/activate it. The manual test URL is different from the production URL.

**A node shows a red triangle right after import**
Cause: No credential is attached yet.
Fix: Expected on a fresh import — open the node and attach a credential (see the Credentials note).

**Writes fail with 422 UNKNOWN_FIELD_NAME**
Cause: The Airtable column names don't match the ones mapped here.
Fix: Airtable field names are case-sensitive. Rename either the columns or the Set/upsert mappings so they line up exactly.

**Duplicate rows for one order**
Cause: No 'Order ID' column is chosen as the matching column, so upsert can't match.
Fix: Keep Order ID in matchingColumns; that's what makes a re-delivered webhook update instead of insert.

**Provider returns 429**
Cause: You are hitting the API rate limit.
Fix: The node already retries with backoff; widen the schedule interval or lower the batch size to stay under quota.

Still stuck? The **Executions** tab shows the exact node that failed and the data going into it — start there.

## Design decisions

Upsert matches on Order ID because Shopify delivers webhooks at-least-once — the same order can arrive twice, and matching on a stable key turns a replay into an update instead of a duplicate. Line items are flattened to a single readable string because Airtable cells hold text far more happily than nested JSON. Failures go to an Airtable errors table (not just an alert) so a failed order is replayable, not merely reported.

## Practice exercises

Already production-shaped — deepen it:

1. Add a linked 'Customer' table and link each order to its buyer.
2. Also subscribe to orders/updated so status changes flow through the same upsert.
3. Add a formula field in Airtable that flags high-value orders for review.
